courses.title: Pharmacotherapy II
courses.description: Evidence-based pharmacotherapy of infectious diseases, HIV, oncology, psychiatric and neurological disorders, and pain management, with pharmaceutical care plans.

topics.title: Antimicrobial Therapy and Stewardship
topics.summary: Principles of antimicrobial selection, common infections, and stewardship.

material.heading: Principles
material.body: Antimicrobial selection considers the likely organism (empirical therapy based on site and local antibiogram), culture and sensitivity results (definitive therapy — de-escalate to narrow spectrum), patient factors (allergy, age, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, site penetration — e.g. CNS), drug factors (spectrum, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics — time-dependent killing for beta-lactams, concentration-dependent for aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones), cost and resistance. Take cultures before starting antibiotics where possible. Switch IV to oral when the patient is improving and can absorb (IV-to-oral switch). Define duration (shorter courses are often as effective). The WHO AWaRe classification groups antibiotics into Access (first-line, e.g. amoxicillin), Watch (higher resistance potential, e.g. ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin) and Reserve (last resort, e.g. colistin, linezolid).

material.heading: Common infections and stewardship
material.body: Examples (adult, Nigerian guidelines vary): community-acquired pneumonia — amoxicillin (mild) or ceftriaxone plus a macrolide (severe); uncomplicated UTI — nitrofurantoin; typhoid — ciprofloxacin (resistance rising), ceftriaxone or azithromycin; gonorrhoea — ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; bacterial meningitis — high-dose ceftriaxone. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is driven by overuse, self-medication, over-the-counter sales, poor infection control and substandard drugs; Nigeria's National Action Plan on AMR follows a One Health approach. Antimicrobial stewardship programmes (ASP) — led by infectious disease physicians, clinical pharmacists and microbiologists — use prospective audit and feedback, formulary restriction, guidelines, education and monitoring of consumption (defined daily doses) to optimise use.
keyPoints: AMR National Action Plan: One Health

topics.title: HIV, Tuberculosis and Malaria Pharmacotherapy
topics.summary: Antiretroviral regimens, TB treatment, antimalarials and key interactions and toxicities.

material.heading: HIV
material.body: Nigerian guidelines recommend a preferred first-line regimen of TLD — tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + lamivudine + dolutegravir — for adults and adolescents, started as soon as possible after diagnosis (rapid ART, including same day). Children use weight-appropriate dolutegravir-based regimens (paediatric DTG 10 mg dispersible). Monitoring: viral load at 6 and 12 months then annually (target < 1,000 copies/mL; ideally undetectable), with enhanced adherence counselling for high viral load. Toxicities: tenofovir — renal impairment and bone loss (check creatinine); dolutegravir — insomnia, weight gain, raised creatinine (inhibits tubular secretion without real GFR change); efavirenz — CNS effects; zidovudine — anaemia; abacavir — hypersensitivity (HLA-B*5701). Rifampicin induces dolutegravir metabolism, so DTG is given twice daily with rifampicin. Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and TB preventive therapy (isoniazid or 3HP) are part of care.

material.heading: TB and malaria
material.body: Drug-susceptible TB: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (2HRZE) then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (4HR), as fixed-dose combinations with directly observed or supported therapy; pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy. Toxicities: hepatotoxicity (H, R, Z), orange body fluids (R), optic neuritis (E), hyperuricaemia/gout (Z). Drug-resistant TB uses all-oral regimens such as BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) for 6 months. Malaria: uncomplicated — artemether–lumefantrine (take with fatty food) or artesunate–amodiaquine; severe — IV or IM artesunate (at least 24 hours, then a full ACT course); pre-referral rectal artesunate for children; pregnancy — ACTs are now recommended in all trimesters (including the first); IPTp with SP from the second trimester. Primaquine (G6PD testing) for P. vivax radical cure is rarely needed in Nigeria (mostly P. falciparum).

topics.title: Oncology Pharmacotherapy
topics.summary: Principles of chemotherapy, common regimens in Nigeria, toxicities and supportive care.

material.heading: Principles
material.body: Cancer chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells; drugs may be cell cycle-specific (antimetabolites — methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, capecitabine; vinca alkaloids — vincristine; taxanes — paclitaxel, docetaxel) or cell cycle-non-specific (alkylating agents — cyclophosphamide; platinum compounds — cisplatin, carboplatin; anthracyclines — doxorubicin). Combination chemotherapy uses drugs with different mechanisms and non-overlapping toxicities. Treatment intent may be curative, adjuvant (after surgery), neoadjuvant (before surgery), or palliative. Doses are calculated by body surface area (carboplatin by AUC using the Calvert formula). Targeted therapies (trastuzumab for HER2-positive breast cancer, imatinib for CML — supported by patient access programmes in Nigeria) and hormonal therapies (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer; androgen deprivation for prostate cancer) are important. Breast, cervical and prostate cancers are the most common in Nigeria.

material.heading: Toxicities and supportive care
material.body: Common toxicities: myelosuppression (neutropenia — nadir 7–14 days; febrile neutropenia is an emergency requiring immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics), nausea and vomiting (prevent with 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron, dexamethasone, and NK1 antagonists like aprepitant for highly emetogenic regimens e.g. cisplatin), mucositis, alopecia, and drug-specific toxicities: doxorubicin — cardiotoxicity (cumulative dose limit), cisplatin — nephrotoxicity (hydration), ototoxicity; vincristine — neuropathy (never intrathecal — fatal); cyclophosphamide — haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna); methotrexate — mucositis and myelosuppression (leucovorin rescue); bleomycin — pulmonary fibrosis; tumour lysis syndrome (hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase). Safe handling of cytotoxics, extravasation management, pain control and nutrition are pharmacist responsibilities.

topics.title: Psychiatric and Neurological Pharmacotherapy
topics.summary: Depression, psychosis, bipolar disorder, epilepsy and Parkinson's disease treatment.

material.heading: Psychiatric disorders
material.body: Depression: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram) are first-line; effects take 2–4 weeks; continue for at least 6–12 months after remission; watch for early activation and suicidality in young people; amitriptyline (TCA — dangerous in overdose, anticholinergic effects) is cheap and common in Nigeria. Psychosis/schizophrenia: first-generation antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine; long-acting fluphenazine decanoate depot — widely used in Nigeria) cause extrapyramidal side effects (acute dystonia — treat with anticholinergics like benzhexol/procyclidine; akathisia; parkinsonism; tardive dyskinesia) and hyperprolactinaemia; second-generation (risperidone, olanzapine) have fewer EPSEs but metabolic effects (weight gain, diabetes); clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (agranulocytosis — FBC monitoring). Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is an emergency. Bipolar disorder: lithium (narrow therapeutic range 0.4–1.0 mmol/L; toxicity — tremor, confusion; interactions with NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors), valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential), carbamazepine.

material.heading: Neurological disorders
material.body: Epilepsy: choose by seizure type — generalised seizures: sodium valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential), lamotrigine, levetiracetam; focal seizures: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam; phenobarbital remains widely used in Nigeria for affordability. Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) reduce contraceptive efficacy. Phenytoin has non-linear (saturable) kinetics and a narrow therapeutic range. Status epilepticus: benzodiazepine first (IV lorazepam/diazepam or buccal midazolam), then a second-line agent (phenytoin/fosphenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam, or phenobarbital). Parkinson's disease: levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa/benserazide) is most effective; long-term 'wearing-off' and dyskinesias; dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors; avoid dopamine antagonists like metoclopramide and haloperidol.
keyPoints: Valproate: avoid in women of childbearing potential

topics.title: Pain Management and Palliative Care
topics.summary: WHO analgesic ladder, opioids, neuropathic pain and palliative symptom control.

material.heading: Analgesia
material.body: Pain assessment uses scales (numeric, visual analogue, faces for children). The WHO analgesic approach (originally a three-step ladder for cancer pain): step 1 non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs) ± adjuvants; step 2 weak opioids (codeine, tramadol) or low-dose strong opioids; step 3 strong opioids (morphine — gold standard; oxycodone, fentanyl patches) — 'by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual, with attention to detail'. Adjuvants for neuropathic pain: amitriptyline, gabapentin/pregabalin, carbamazepine (trigeminal neuralgia). NSAIDs: gastrointestinal bleeding (use PPI cover), renal impairment, cardiovascular risk; avoid in late pregnancy. Opioid adverse effects: constipation (always co-prescribe a laxative), nausea, sedation, respiratory depression (naloxone reverses); tolerance and dependence differ from addiction. Paracetamol overdose causes hepatotoxicity — N-acetylcysteine is the antidote.

material.heading: Palliative care
material.body: Palliative care improves quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illness through prevention and relief of suffering — pain and other physical, psychosocial and spiritual problems. Nigeria has limited palliative services and poor access to oral morphine (among the lowest per-capita opioid consumption globally), partly due to regulatory barriers and opiophobia; oral morphine solution compounded from powder in hospitals (e.g. Hospice and Palliative Care centres) improves access. Symptom control: breathlessness (low-dose opioids, fan, positioning), nausea (metoclopramide, haloperidol, cyclizine by cause), constipation, anorexia, anxiety, and terminal secretions (hyoscine butylbromide). Breakthrough pain doses are about one-sixth of the 24-hour regular dose. Converting routes: oral morphine to subcutaneous is approximately 2:1. Communication, advance care planning and bereavement support are essential.
